title: Sparse genotypes and Firth correction

blocks.what_we_do: Compare an ordinary fit with a Firth fit that we force at one low-frequency autosomal variant. The variant is one of the retained variants.
blocks.why: A rare genotype can have very few cases or controls. The ordinary logistic fit uses [maximum likelihood](docs/glossary.md#maximum-likelihood). It chooses the coefficients that make the observed outcomes most likely under the model. Sometimes one genotype group contains only cases or only controls. This is separation, and the coefficient can then grow without limit. [Firth correction](docs/glossary.md#firth-regression) reduces the bias of small samples and can give finite estimates. It does not add information. It does not fix confounding, wrong genotype calls or a poor study design. The main scan of this dataset did not need the Firth fallback. We force Firth here so that you can compare the two results at one variant. Variants below the 1% frequency filter do not come back.
blocks.you_need: The final cohort, the main results from 6.4 and the covariates from 6.3.
blocks.command:
```{r s6-6}
results <- guided_association(guided_path(cfg, "6.4", "association"))
minor <- pmin(results$A1_FREQ, 1 - results$A1_FREQ)
candidates <- which(results$CHROM %in% as.character(1:22) & valid_p(results$P) & minor > 0)
chosen <- results$ID[candidates[which.min(minor[candidates])]]
guided_list(chosen, guided_path(cfg, "6.6", "variant.txt"))
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "5.7"), "--snp", chosen, "--covar", guided_path(cfg, "6.3", "covariates.tsv"),
  "--covar-name", "Age,PC1-PC10", "--covar-variance-standardize", "--glm", "firth", "sex", "hide-covar", "--out", guided_path(cfg, "6.6", "firth")))
comparison <- guided_association(guided_path(cfg, "6.6", "firth"))
print(results[results$ID == chosen, c("ID", "A1", "OR", "P")])
print(comparison[, c("ID", "A1", "OR", "P")])
stopifnot(nrow(comparison) == 1L, valid_p(comparison$P))
```

Plain PLINK 2 command (use `bin\plink2.exe` on Windows):

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s5-7_state --extract results/guided/s6-6_variant.txt --covar results/guided/s6-3_covariates.tsv --covar-name Age,PC1-PC10 --covar-variance-standardize --glm firth sex hide-covar --out results/guided/s6-6_firth --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

The R command uses `--snp` with the chosen ID. The terminal command uses `--extract` with a file that holds this one ID. `--glm firth` asks for Firth correction at this variant, without waiting for the fallback. The covariate options and the resource options are the same as at 6.4. `--pfile` reads the final genotype files. `--out` sets the prefix of the report files. `--threads 2` limits PLINK to two worker threads. `--memory 2048` gives PLINK 2048 MiB (about 2 GB) of working memory.
blocks.expected_result:
One forced Firth result with a finite value, next to the ordinary estimate from the main scan for the same A1 allele. Small differences in the numbers are normal. Forced Firth is not a better scan for the whole genome.

The tested PLINK version is defined in `config.R` and recorded in
`software_versions.txt`. Validation: executable chunks passed on Windows; main test counts and significance match the expected values.
blocks.troubleshooting: Stop at the first error. Check the input file named in the message and the previous step. Keep the command and the console log. Do not use files from a different version of the dataset. See [troubleshooting](docs/troubleshooting.md).
blocks.quick_check:
Does Firth correction make an association precise when it rests on very few carriers?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

No. It makes the fit more stable, but the uncertainty can stay large.

</details>
blocks.files_created: The chosen variant ID, the forced Firth report and the log files.
blocks.under_the_hood:
**What the tool computes.** Ordinary logistic regression chooses the coefficients that maximise the likelihood. Firth regression maximises a penalised likelihood instead: it adds half the log-determinant of the Fisher information (the Jeffreys prior). This removes the leading term of the small-sample bias and keeps the estimates finite. When one genotype group holds only cases or only controls, the ordinary estimate does not exist. The report gives `OR` (the exponential of the coefficient for the `A1` allele), the standard error of the log odds ratio, the Z statistic and `P`. PLINK 2 reports an asymptotic p-value from the Wald Z statistic, also for Firth fits.

**Why these values.** The main scan used `firth-fallback`, PLINK's default, which switches to Firth only when the ordinary fit fails. We force `firth` once so you can compare. The 1% frequency filter keeps the rarest variants out of the scan.

**Pitfalls.** Firth shrinks estimates towards no effect and gives no new information. With few carriers the Wald p-value can mislead. Penalised likelihood ratio tests and profile confidence intervals are often preferable to the Wald test. For low-count variants (roughly fewer than 400 minor alleles), simulations favour a Firth likelihood ratio test over the plain Wald, score or likelihood ratio tests in joint analysis. PLINK 2 reports a Wald p-value from the Firth fit instead, so treat borderline results with care. Always look at the carrier counts and doubt genotype calls at rare variants. The spelling `--covar-variance-standardize` is American; the course text says standardise.

**References**

1. Firth D (1993) Bias reduction of maximum likelihood estimates. Biometrika 80:27-38. doi:10.1093/biomet/80.1.27.
2. Albert A, Anderson JA (1984) On the existence of maximum likelihood estimates in logistic regression models. Biometrika 71:1-10. doi:10.1093/biomet/71.1.1.
3. Heinze G, Schemper M (2002) A solution to the problem of separation in logistic regression. Stat Med 21:2409-2419. PMID 12210625.
4. Ma C et al. (2013) Recommended joint and meta-analysis strategies for case-control association testing of single low-count variants. Genet Epidemiol 37:539-550. PMID 23788246.
